lead: The third law gives entropy a fixed zero. For a perfect ordered crystal at absolute zero, S = 0. Then every absolute entropy can be found by heating the substance from 0 K and summing C<sub>p</sub>/T. This sounds abstract, but it is how entropy tables are built. It also explains why some solids keep a small leftover entropy after cooling, and why no laboratory reaches 0 K exactly. Engineers use it to compare absolute entropies in power cycles, refrigerators and chemical reactions.
prereq: You need: entropy and the Clausius inequality and heat capacity from the first-law chapters.

sections.h3: The third law and the Nernst theorem

blocks.text: Absolute zero is 0 K, about −273.15 °C. A perfect crystal is a solid with every atom or molecule in one ordered arrangement, with no frozen-in disorder. The Nernst heat theorem says that for condensed phases near absolute zero, the entropy change of a reversible isothermal process tends to zero as T → 0. In plain form, the third law states: the entropy of a perfect ordered crystal is zero at 0 K.

This is a reference point, not a calculation trick. Before the third law, entropy changes could be measured but absolute entropy had no origin. The law chooses S(0 K) = 0 for the perfect crystal. Then S at any T is an absolute entropy. Tables of standard molar entropy, S°, use this choice. The value at 298.15 K is not zero, and 0 °C is not the zero either. Only 0 K is.

The law applies to a perfect crystal. A real crystal can have defects, mixed orientations or frozen disorder. Those solids may have residual entropy at 0 K. The next sections separate the ideal case from these real cases.
For reversible heating at constant pressure, dS = C<sub>p</sub> dT / T. Start at 0 K with S(0) = 0 and integrate to T:

blocks.where: S(T) is absolute molar entropy at T in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T′ is the integration variable, running from 0 K up to the final temperature T in K; C<sub>p</sub> is heat capacity at constant pressure in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; ΔH<sub>tr</sub> is the enthalpy of a phase transition in J mol⁻¹ and T<sub>tr</sub> its temperature in K. The sum adds each solid–solid, melting or boiling transition between 0 K and T, and the integral is taken piece by piece over each single-phase range.

blocks.text: The integral cannot start at exactly 0 K in a real measurement, because C<sub>p</sub>/T is hard to measure and 0 K is unattainable. Experimenters measure C<sub>p</sub> down to a low temperature, often a few kelvin. Below that they fit the low-temperature law C<sub>p</sub> = aT³. Then the integral from 0 K to that low temperature T is finite and easy: ∫₀<sup>T</sup> aT′² dT′ = aT³/3, which is one third of C<sub>p</sub> at T. Here a is a constant with units J mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴. The cubic form is the Debye T³ law. Strictly it is a law for C<sub>V</sub>, but at a few kelvin C<sub>P</sub> and C<sub>V</sub> of a solid differ by far less than the measurement error, so C<sub>P</sub> = aT³ is used. Metals add an electronic term: C<sub>P</sub> = aT³ + γT, which integrates to S = aT³/3 + γT.
Procedure to build an absolute entropy:

items: Measure C<sub>p</sub> at many temperatures above the lowest measured point.
Fit C<sub>p</sub> = aT³ below that point and add aT³/3.
Add ΔH<sub>tr</sub>/T<sub>tr</sub> for every phase transition on the path.
Report S(T) with the third-law zero at 0 K.

blocks.text: This is why entropy tables need heat-capacity data, not just one calorimeter reading.

sections.h3: Residual entropy and the unattainable zero

blocks.text: Residual entropy is entropy that remains at 0 K when a solid is not a perfect ordered crystal. Carbon monoxide is the standard example. The molecules CO are almost symmetric in size, so in a crystal they can point CO or OC with little energy difference. Cooling freezes a random arrangement. The crystal has S(0) > 0: if the two orientations were equally likely it would be R ln 2 = 8.314 × 0.693 = 5.76 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; the measured residual entropy of CO is a little smaller, about 4.6 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, because the freezing is not perfectly random. Glasses are another case: a liquid's disorder is frozen in before it can crystallize, so the glass keeps extra entropy.

The third law needs the words perfect crystal. For CO, glass or a crystal with frozen defects, S(0) is not zero. The law still sets the zero for the perfectly ordered reference, and the measured entropy of the real solid is larger by the residual amount.

The third law also says absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps. As a system is cooled toward 0 K, each step removes less entropy and the cooling power falls. A real cryostat can reach very low temperatures, but it cannot cross to 0 K. This is the unattainability statement. It is consistent with S → 0: at 0 K the entropy would be fixed, and no finite process can take a system there. In engineering, the practical message is that reaching lower temperatures costs more work and better insulation; see refrigeration and liquefaction.

examples.question: A crystal obeys C<sub>p</sub> = aT³ at low temperature with a = 0.001 J mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴. Using S(0) = 0, find S at 10 K.
steps: Identify the low-temperature heat capacity: C<sub>p</sub> = aT³, with a = 0.001 J mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴.
Use the third-law integral: S(10 K) − S(0 K) = ∫₀¹⁰ (C<sub>p</sub>/T) dT.
Set S(0 K) = 0 for the perfect crystal.
Integrate: S(10 K) = ∫₀¹⁰ aT² dT = a[T³/3]₀¹⁰ = a(1000/3) K³.
Insert a: S = 0.001 × 1000/3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.3333 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

examples.question: Build the absolute molar entropy of a substance at 298.15 K and 1 bar from these data. Below 10 K the solid follows C<sub>p</sub> = aT³, and C<sub>p</sub>(10 K) = 0.80 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. From 10 K to the melting point 200 K, the tabulated integral ∫C<sub>p</sub>/T dT for the solid is 60.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. ΔH<sub>fus</sub> = 8.00 kJ/mol at 200 K. The liquid has C<sub>p</sub> = 120 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ from 200 K to 298.15 K.
steps: Debye part, 0 to 10 K: S = aT³/3 = C<sub>p</sub>(10 K)/3 = 0.80/3 = 0.27 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Solid, 10 K to 200 K: 60.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (given).
Melting at 200 K: ΔH<sub>fus</sub>/T<sub>m</sub> = 8000/200 = 40.0 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Add, with S(0) = 0 for the perfect crystal: S = 0.27 + 60.0 + 40.0 + 47.9 = 148.2 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
examples.answer: S(298.15 K) = 148.2 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; the melting step alone gives 40.0 of it.

traps: Using S = 0 at 0 °C or at 298 K. The third-law zero is 0 K, not the ice point or room temperature.
Forgetting to divide C<sub>p</sub> by T. The entropy integral is ∫(C<sub>p</sub>/T)dT, not ∫C<sub>p</sub> dT.
Assuming every solid has S(0) = 0. Only a perfect ordered crystal does; CO and glasses keep residual entropy.
Omitting phase-transition terms. A complete absolute entropy adds ΔH<sub>tr</sub>/T<sub>tr</sub> at each transition between 0 K and T.
Thinking enough cooling steps can reach exactly 0 K. The third law says 0 K is unattainable in a finite number of steps.

quiz.q: State the third law for a perfect crystal.
quiz.a: For a perfect ordered crystal, S → 0 as T → 0 K; at 0 K its entropy is taken as zero.

quiz.q: Why is S(0) not zero for a CO crystal?
quiz.a: CO molecules can freeze in two orientations. The frozen random arrangement adds residual entropy, so the crystal is not perfectly ordered.

quiz.q: A solid obeys C<sub>p</sub> = aT³ with a = 0.002 J mol⁻¹ K⁻⁴. Use S(0) = 0. Find S at 5 K.
quiz.a: S = ∫₀⁵ aT² dT = aT³/3 = 0.002 × 125/3 = 0.0833 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

quiz.q: A glass has residual entropy 5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Does this violate the third law? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The third law's zero applies to a perfect ordered crystal. The glass is disordered, so its measured S(0) is above the reference zero by the residual entropy.

quiz.q: Why do entropy tables use 0 K rather than 298 K as the reference?
quiz.a: The third law fixes S = 0 at 0 K for a perfect crystal. A 298 K reference would be arbitrary and would hide the absolute entropy.

quiz.q: For C<sub>p</sub> = aT³, show that S = aT³/3 when S(0) = 0.
Why can absolute zero not be reached in a finite number of cooling steps?
quiz.a: Each cooling step (for example an adiabatic demagnetisation) removes entropy by switching a control variable at low temperature. Near 0 K the entropy curves for the two settings of that variable come together, because every S tends to the same value there. Each step therefore removes less entropy and lowers T by a smaller fraction, so an infinite number of steps would be needed to reach 0 K.

beyond: Not for the exam. The third law underpins low-temperature metrology and the entropy tables used in cryogenics and chemical process design. Research on residual entropy appears in glassy pharmaceuticals, where frozen disorder affects stability, and in magnetic materials with spin ice. Absolute-zero experiments search for new cooling methods and for quantum limits on refrigeration. Search next for Nernst heat theorem, residual entropy, and unattainability of absolute zero.
